title: Supreme Court Says: If You're Born in the USA, You're a Citizen!
summary: Have you ever wondered what makes someone a citizen of a country? In the United States, if you're born here, you're automatically a citizen — no matter where your parents are from. That's been the rule for over 150 years, thanks to the 14th Amendment to the Constitution. But President Donald Trump tried to change that. He signed an order saying babies born to undocumented immigrants or some temporary visitors shouldn't get citizenship. The Supreme Court just said no. In a 6-3 decision, the justices ruled that the Constitution is clear: anyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen at birth. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that citizenship is "the right to have rights" and that the court was keeping a promise made long ago. President Trump called the decision "too bad" and wants Congress to pass a new law. But changing the Constitution is really hard. Civil rights groups cheered the ruling. One lawyer said it "solidifies what we have known to be true for over a hundred years." So for now, the old rule stands: born in the USA? You're a citizen!
why_it_matters: This decision means that if you or a friend were born in the United States, you are automatically a citizen no matter where your parents came from—a rule that shapes who you are and your rights.

questions.question: What does the 14th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution say?
options: a) Only children of U.S. citizens can be citizens.
b) Anyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen at birth.
c) The president decides who becomes a citizen.
d) Citizenship must be earned through a test.
questions.correct_answer: b) Anyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen at birth.

questions.question: What did President Donald Trump's order try to do?
options: a) Give bonus citizenship to babies born in hospitals
b) Stop babies of undocumented immigrants from getting automatic citizenship
c) Only allow citizenship for people from Europe
d) Delay citizenship until age 18
questions.correct_answer: b) Stop babies of undocumented immigrants from getting automatic citizenship

questions.question: How did the Supreme Court rule on birthright citizenship?
options: a) 6-3 to keep the rule that being born in the U.S. makes you a citizen
b) 9-0 to change the Constitution
c) They tied and could not decide.
d) They refused to hear the case.
questions.correct_answer: a) 6-3 to keep the rule that being born in the U.S. makes you a citizen

questions.question: What did Chief Justice John Roberts write about citizenship?
options: a) It is 'the right to vote' only.
b) It is 'the right to have rights'.
c) It is not important for most people.
d) It should be decided by each state.
questions.correct_answer: b) It is 'the right to have rights'.

questions.question: Why can't President Trump easily change the citizenship rule?
options: a) Because the Supreme Court agrees with him
b) Because changing the Constitution is very difficult
c) Because Congress can do it with a simple vote
d) Because the president has full power over the Constitution
questions.correct_answer: b) Because changing the Constitution is very difficult

questions.question: How did civil rights groups react to the Supreme Court ruling?
options: a) They protested loudly.
b) They cheered the decision.
c) They ignored the ruling.
d) They asked the president for a new order.

background_read: The 14th Amendment was added to the Constitution in 1868 after the Civil War to make sure that everyone born in the United States—including formerly enslaved people—became citizens.
President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) wanted to change who could become a citizen just by being born in the country.
The Supreme Court is the top court in America; it has nine justices who decide whether laws follow the Constitution.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Donald Trump, the Supreme Court justices (including Chief Justice John Roberts), civil rights groups
WHAT: President Trump's order to deny citizenship to some babies born in the U.S. was struck down by a 6-3 Supreme Court decision that upheld birthright citizenship under the 14th Amendment.
WHY: Because the Constitution has guaranteed birthright citizenship for over 150 years, and the court decided that promise must be protected even when a president wants to change it.

perspectives.description: They celebrate the ruling as a protection of a basic promise of fairness and equality, saying it keeps America a country where anyone born here truly belongs.
They think birthright citizenship should not apply when parents are undocumented or only visiting, and they want Congress to pass a new law to change how citizenship works at birth.
They point out that the 14th Amendment was created to heal a divided nation and has been a bedrock of American life for over a century, so changing it would be a huge step.
